descriptionChirho: To physically carry or bring something or someone out of a place, including carrying out the dead for burial (Acts 5) and bringing out persons. Spanish uses 'sacar' (take out) and 'llevar' (carry), Arabic uses 'ḥāmilīn' (حاملين, carrying) and 'akhrajahu' (أخرجه, he brought out), Korean uses 'nallaseo' (날라서, carrying) and 'gajyeogara' (가져오라, bring), Hindi uses 'le gayā' (ले गया, took away), and Swahili uses '-beba nje' (carry outside) and '-peleka' (send/take). The physical transport sense is consistent across aorist, future, and imperative forms.

To produce or yield fruit or vegetation, used metaphorically of land or plants bringing forth growth. Spanish uses 'que produce' (that produces), Arabic uses 'mukhrijatan' (مُخْرِجَةً, producing/bringing forth), Hindi uses 'utpann karne vālī' (उत्पन्न करने वाली, one that produces), Korean uses 'naeneun' (내는, yielding), and Swahili uses '-zaa' (bear fruit/give birth). This agricultural/botanical sense is semantically distinct from physically carrying objects out of a location.
